comments.value: The text is longer and more messy than I expected. Therefore, later, I will probably make some changes and comments.

While I do agree with you on points one and two, I have to disagree on point three, and point four kinda falls away with my stance on point three.

When I first heard about Udon, I was very sceptical.  But once I saw the existance of Udon Assembly (which I'll refer to as Udon Intermediate Language, or UIL, because that's closer to what it actually is) that they seem to be open in terms of architecture, including outright ecouraging external compilers, I did see a spark of hope.  It leads me to think that, perhaps, someone on the team had actually taken a compiler course, and there was hope for them yet.

There are many posts talking about defining structures, or adding opcodes for arithemetic operations, etc.  They are all missing the point.  Those are all abstractions.  It doesn't matter if you have one structured variable, or a dozen non-structured ones. It doesn't matter if you have 100 opcodes all doing different things, or ten opcodes and all of the interesting things are what amount to function calls.  Any decent compiler can optimize for all of that.  Do you think that the C executable running knows or cares whether the int it's doing calculations on is in a structure? No. It just knows "add the value in this register to that register and put it in this other register" or "get this value from this spot in memory and put it here".  It doesn't care if the code it's executing exists in a subroutine, or a method, or a lambda, or a closure, or any of the dozens of things that all basically mean the same thing in practice.

It doesn't matter (for the most part) if the IL uses three opcodes to add two numbers, or thirty.  The only place where that matters is in the compiler.  If the compiler is good, it'll get rid of all of the extra and boil it down to the exact bytecodes that need to be sent to the processor to accompish the task at hand.

We should also bear in mind that speed is not the only design concern here.  Safety is another important design concern.  If these programs are transmitted in IL, and compiled in place on the client side, ensures that the barrier toward getting malicious executable code running in the process space is much higher.  All of this talk about "just allow C# scripts" seems to miss this point.  Yes, it's certainly possible to scan C# source, or compiled CIL, to see if anything looks suspcious, but it is not an easy task.  The only options down that road are either to A) allow for the possibility of malicious code, which is completely unacceptable; B) require C# scripts be so simple that they might as well be this node-based language we're already complaining about; or C) spend significant amounts of time and resources writing an execution analysis engine that might not even be possible (see also, the Halting Problem).  That's not even getting into the problems associated with trying to write code for execution on multiple platforms (in this case, .NET and Android).

Or, you design your own IL.  You can design that IL to preclude most of the actively harmful things that a malicious party could do.  And then when you compile that IL into executable code it's quite easy to insert your own code to guard against those situations which are harder to detect with code analysis.  And then you can compile it at runtime to the appropriate platform.

For an example of that, look at infinite loops. Having loops available in the language is very useful, but having infinite loops is difficult.  Now, if the language is interpreted, then infinite loops are easily delt with; the interpreter simply stops after a period of time.  But of course, interpretation is not desirable from a speed perspective.  When the language is compiled directly, it's much more difficult to see if a loop is infinite. I'm not saying that can't be managed, but it's a lot more difficult.  With a custom compiled IL (especially one as basic as UIL), the compiler can insert code before every JUMP instruction that moves backwards in the file.  Then, if this code is executed too many times, it can be interuppted by the runtime, just as in the interpreted case, but without the added overhead.

Of course, all of this assumes that UIL will be compiled at some point.  While I know from my own experience that this is entirly possible (the ERP [Enterprise Resource Planning] software I wrote and have actively maintained for the last ten years uses the same techniques that could be used in this situation), I do assume that the devs will be using these techniques.  I understand that this is not a safe assumption.  I saw a glimmer of hope; I've not yet seen proof of hope.

I recommend to anyone who's interested in compiler design, "Compilers: Principles, Techniques, and Tools" by Aho, Sethi, and Ullman (And Lam) (1st ed: 9780201100884, 2nd ed: 9780321486813), which I've found to be an invaluable resource over the years.  While the second edition might be newer, I've gotten quite a lot of use out of the first edition, which can be had on Amazon for as little as $4.


As for your list of suggestions (in order):

- Many of these abstractions can (and I'm confidant, will) be provided by compiler writers.

- Execution path should only be for nodes that have non-deterministic or time-relevant side-effects.  If anything, this means that fewer nodes should have execution path arrows.  This current node language has a fair bit of functional aspect to it.

- Again, this will be delt with by compilers.

- Syntactic sugar, but still a good suggestion.

- Not sure what this one means.

- Absolutely not, for the reasons explained above.

- See above.

When it comes to the nodes, I largely agree; while I'd have preferred they provide a text language from the start, their node based system could definitely use a lot of the same features commonly found in text languages (structs, function definitions, etc.) My only quibble would be with #2; node based languages naturally lean toward a functional paradigm, and in such paradigms the actual order of execution doesn't particularly matter as long as you get the correct answer at the end.  The only reason to even have the execution flow at all is either for control flow, or because of timing.

(Wow, Canny's comment editing leaves a lot to be desired...)

With the VM, yes, I agree it's complicated, but I think in the long run, if it's implemented correctly (big if) it could actually represent a simplification of the overall program. (I've definitely experienced that firsthand in my own work.)

@{5b93e4741e75674a7ea03e2f|full_name}: 
"Those are all abstractions."
I agree that structures are completely abstract and irrelevant to bytecode, but arithmetic is neither abstract nor irrelevant. Efficient iterators and arrays (particularly safe arrays) require mathematics to be fast. Maybe you were thinking of arithmetic from the point of view of C#, where you can perform it on non-primitives and is therefore often very abstract.

"It doesn't matter (for the most part) if the IL uses three opcodes to add two numbers, or thirty."
The opcode parser would be O(1) complexity, so I'm not sure why you think something taking 10x longer doesn't matter. Though I think I get what you're really trying to get across when it comes to more abstracts ops that have a longer running time than opcode parsing (ie. CISC ops). With a RISC op, the time it takes to process that op in bytecode should be nearly as long running the op itself. This what the RISC arch endeavors to accomplish.

So comparing an ADD op to what UdonVM must currently do, it would be 4 ops (3 pushes + extern) vs 1. This would be a 4x increase in the time to complete. Which you could argue is 4x an insignificant number (nanoseconds maybe), but if it really is so arbitrary a choice as you suggest why would you choose 1/4 performance?

Because I'm assuming that the UIL is ultimately going to be compiled in some fashion.  Yeah there's a UdonVM interpreter, but that's quite likely to be just for testing. It might be just for the editor's sake; or maybe it does run on that right now... But this is an alpha.

It is important to remember that in a compiled environment, 2x opcodes does not necessarily mean 2x slower; and 1/2x opcodes does not necessarily mean 2x faster.  The UIL opcodes can be used to build an expression tree; that tree can be optimized, and the resulting tree be compiled. That's how many modern compilers work, especially with IL languages (.NET, Java, etc).

And the time to compile is not particularly important either; once it's compiled, it's compiled.  It's time to run that's important.

(And, BTW, an add in CIL could also potentially take 4 ops.)

Don't get me wrong; I'm not saying that UIL couldn't benefit from more opcodes (I myself would like to see more stack manipulation opcodes, for a start).  I am saying that I can't think of any opcodes that it absolutely must have in order to work, and that getting hung up on the number of opcodes it takes to express an operation is, at this early stage, indicative of premature optimization and should probably be avoided.
Ok, cancel all of that.  I didn't know about IL2CPP, and that apparently JITing isn't just not being done because alpha, but because impossible.

I too am dismayed by how low level this is despite being superficially a graph-based language. I’d almost go to the point of saying that it isn’t a graph-based language at all, but just a different and more annoying way to write C# code.

Do you think we could make a compiler which just takes C# and outputs the required unity asset for an Udon graph? ;D

I mostly agree about complexity of udon, too complicated for newbies, too weird for programmers. Like you even need to cast int to float manually with separate block.

And i somehow agree with most of other points but... allowing raw assemblies would be much much harder. They would still probably need to abstract half of unity engine to not allow any changes to selected components of the scene that could break the game, and you can't check that using static analysis, so it would need to check each method call or build second copy of scene with own types and only safe to work with objects. 
So the vm is the right choice, but sadly due to il2cpp they can't easily compile it to IL and just make the JIT do the job. They could only compile scripts on their own servers, but that could be expensive at large scale.
So imho we either need better VM support for custom types and other more advanced operations or for more ways to access byte arrays/memory would help a lot.

I agree, it's too complex for beginners without Unity & C# experience but too messy for complex programs. The graphs turn into spaghetti quickly and can even start lagging. I hope someone makes a text based compiler for Udon.

VM's are absolutely necessary when you have arbitrary execution and memory allocation capabilities. Udon's graphing system is not necessary to create such a VM. Labview has a big graphing language thats made to largely replicate standard programming languages and does so pretty well - but it's not as a safe VM afaik. Space engineers uses a 'safe' C# scripting system in game, however its actual safety may be dubious. Instead if there more mature secular webassembly (wasm) runtimes I'd advocate for that. 
To my knowledge with a proper wasm runtime you have memory and execution space safety guarantees from both how the instruction set is structured and from the runtime as long as it follows the standard. It would be possible to compile C# into modules that are controlled by the runtimes inherent VM. The control offered by this is complete, you can control down to the instruction, so you can throttle execution, limit memory, etc.
wasm is designed for interopability meaning only the chosen functions are exposed, and a layer can be implimented between for validation of any potentially dangerous usages of .net or unity functions. 

Having access to an actual programming language solves a number of use cases that cannot be predicted and accounted for - they're designed with open capabilities. Most unity development uses C# directly, with most of the tutorials and work done in it. 

With a graphing system you have a long list of things to re-impliment, and the output will still not be what anyone wants. But I can see why they chose to do it, there's a number of programs in this space that do it including Blender, Unreal Engine, CryEngine, etc. It's not a bad idea as long as VRCSDK2 stays around for normal users, and udons features are continually developed.

@{5e168b82752fbd5fe163b021|full_name}: simpler would be to just use Lua, its already highly adopted language in game dev with all features you need for it, and with separate JIT compiler when extra performance is needed.

@{5a4aaf7f758fa46d131cd36b|full_name}: Lua does not have the same level of safety guarantees. The environment around it is also outdated sadly. Lua has been a good choice for game mods, which were already mostly trusted.

@{5e168b82752fbd5fe163b021|full_name}: But its still fairly easy to create simple sandboxed environment in lua with only defined set of possible operations, and its already ready to use solution with a lot of tooling available. You don't need to implement near anything to add lua in safe way to your game. I would not be surprised if there is even a ready to use unity asset that does exactly this.

details:
I understand this is a pretty loud headline, but these are the thoughts that came into my head after meeting Udon.
I will try to explain what makes Udon bad both in pov of the general concept and in pov of implementation. I think it is important to say this right now, becuause Udon is not yet complete and in active development, I hope to influence the way it develops.
Also I am sorry for my English, as I am not English-speeking and I did not happen to learn English thoroughly.
~ ~ ~
First, why flow/node-based programming at all? It seems, the main goal of developers is to make a simple mechanism for creating game logic that will allow a wide range of creators to quickly and without special knowledge to implement their ideas.
In practice, it turns out that you still need to know the basics of C# and programming in general. It's not that you need to know the Unity Scripting API, of course, for Unity you need to know this. The point is that Udon stands on C#/Mono, and this is clearly visible in Udon programs. Now Udon looks like an alternative and not complete syntax for C#/CIL, it does not give the opportunity to abstract from C# internals and standards. It does not gives you simple types such as simple integer and floating numbers, strings, lists and tables as it in popular scripting languages such as python/lua/js/..., instead of it gives you full-range of internal types with own low-level specifics (and actually not all of it acessible right now), It does not gives you simple ways to play with collections and opertaions, such as foreach/where/select...  (and actually no collections at all right now), It does not gives you abstract simple and helpful functions/methods (for now). It is literraly asks you to call each (internal) operation manually and you need to know how to do that. It's like you re-writing CIL bytecode visually.
So, what we got? For newbies Udon is too complex. I heared from a lot of friends both who does not have real programming experience, and who have some lua/js/python experience, that Udon is too complex and hard to understand. On the other hand, I see there is a lot of skilled people in community who mostly understands Udon, but they complain about visual programming. For them it's much easier to write text. We already see how ppl trying to make own ways to generate Udon asm to avoid visual scripting at all. (Thank you guys, my respects for your work) It really harder to make some complex logics visually, than by writing text.

~ ~ ~

Second, let's compare node/visual with same for shaders. I often hear Udon comparisons with things as Shader Graph (in future Unities), Amplify Sheder Editor, Shader Forge, Unreal Engine shader editor and similar. Well... Shaders (common) does not have global state while executing, it's is more like microchip code that have entire enironment to play with. So, for example, If I use any fuction such as UnityObjectToClipPos multiple times on same data, HLSL compiller can optimize it into single call, because these function calls doesn't change anything globally. More of that, even if it changes something, compiller can deal with it as all function inlined (in basic shaders w/o new modern fancy features). That's not because HLSL cmpillers super smart or somethig, that's because shading languages have simple design. In Udon/C# stands on Mono, each call is unitary, can change anything globally and compiller can not deal with it and suggest optimizations. Why I pointing this out? For example not so long ago, Error.mdl tried to make one thing that involves file reading ( https://ptb.discordapp.com/channels/189511567539306508/657394924433571870/657813419050795018 , https://cdn.discordapp.com/attachments/657394924433571870/657813411631071242/spagettiknots.jpg ) and noticed it works very slow. If you see carefully, you may notice: there is not obious when "Text Asset Read Bytes" and "Byte[] Get" evaluated, thats problem here (I believe, but sure, as I didn't tested this, lul). But same thing with sahders should works very well. Issue here not with Udon compiller - same can be happen with any other compiller. It's not possible to auto-optimize here, as underlying sofware does not know how these actions affect app environment gloablly. This is a job for programmer. When we writing C# we probably will do something like: byte[] data_that_i_need = my_text_asset_variable.get_bytes(); (Actually just my_text_asset_variable.bytes, as it is property, which is also not obivous, so it is a bad example, but this is another story, I hope u got the point) and then using this data_that_i_need in futher code. In Flow/nodes scripting you have feeling that you can just connect these nodes and that's all, but this is not. You just shoot you leg and didn't noticed how! I want to point out here, that there is actually two kind of flows: data flow and and execution flow, which often non-linear!. Shader basically math-based, developer tells how one color/position vectors should be transformed into other vectors and executing order and path does not (always) matter, and no need to think about global states (as I pointed before), also branhing in shaders very rare. So yea, I want to tell that flow/node based is bad choice for logical programming over global game state. 

You may think: Are you againtst visual programming? Want to force everyone to write text? No. Actually, there is a lot of forms for visual coding. My favorite one design is puzzle-like block nodes, which is popular to teach children the basics of programming. Just google "visual programming", there is a lot of various products!

~ ~ ~

Third, lets talk a bit about Udon ASM and Udon VM. These things. I do not understand why it exist. I have an assumption that devs wanted to create something like a sandbox/security-filter, but instead created monster. I believe this unnecesary layers that create large overhead and way to make 1000 and 1 more hard-to-cathch annoyng bugs in future. More complex something, easier to make misatake, easier to break. For now I don't see what Udon VM can do that is not possible with usual C#/Mono assemblies. You may think? What is another way? You want to allow everyone write whatever they want and execute on other's computers dircetly without any control? Yes and No. You may think it's hard to validate DLLs for various malicious things that creator might make. I want to tell you why it's actually easier than by doing own assembly/compilation/vm system.

Mono assembly is not like common PE assemply. Mono assembly, to put it simple, more like encoded into interpreter-readable usual text-code you writen. It is very high-level abstarction. It does not describes operations on "pure memory" and "pure processor instructions sequence". It is not C/C++, Mono assembly holds a lot of data! It holds everything: types, methods, fields, references to types, references to methods, references to fields, generics, boxing/unboxing and so on, almost no raw data. More of that, there is explicit and strict border between managed and unmanaged, safe and unsafe things. Take a look at any random program writen in C# for Unity (Mono) and take a look at this reference https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_CIL_instructions . Let's ignore basic branch/math/conversion ops, and take a look how program intercats with globals using object-instructions.
Method call? It's call/callvirt, operand type - <method> which is token, which is described in meta of assemly where all references stored. We looking at method this uder this toking and see, for example, creator calling forbidden method. No need to deal with any kind of adresses to strange raw virtual method tables or something. Field access? Same: ldsfld/ldsflda/stfld/stsfld, same: we can see what this token for and check permissions. We see creator using unsafe operaions? Pointers? Allocations? StructLayout? Ban. Easy.
You might think: Isnt its hard to parse assemblies? No. I had experience with Mono.Cecil ( https://www.mono-project.com/docs/tools+libraries/libraries/Mono.Cecil/ ) - it can parse relativly large DLLs into object model for edits or checks in a couple of seconds, even on my weak laptop, basic scripts for worlds should work in fractions of a second, so validation might be both on a server and on a client at world-loading.
I believe, it's much easier to allow scripting for comunity and make CIL opcodes filter, to ban everything complex and perform whitelisting. It's much easier to maintain this, than that large Udon ASM/compiller/VM elephant, and no any extra overhead at runtime! Am I wrong? I suggest to try to write something malicious in comments using only common instructions. For now I know only ways is to make too large arrays and collections, but, I believe same works in Udon (need extra tests).

More of thiat, I know C#/.NET standard provides security control that also covers CIL/MSIL code, which is also supported in Mono. I have no experience with this, so I do not make statements about this. But I know for sure, it's possible to define various security/trust levels and evaluate code with different permissions, to achive somethig like sandboxed envioronment. I going to google more about that so may be I alter this thought.

It hurts me the most that fact community wants to just write C# code, but insted of just build mono assemblies we going to invent own bicycles to generate Udon ASM without any guarantees and support and with risk (as it's unofficial tools), without any way to debug, with higer possiblities of bugs because of complexity, with overhead that will reduce performance, without any cool unique things from UdonVM. It is cool devs allows to make custom asm compillers, but it looks more like: "If u dont like to connect blocks using lines, then here get our instructions set, do what ever you want with these, invent own bicycles, we dont care. And yea we going to change this, so things will randomly got broken in future." I am rly sad and dissapointed about this. 

~ ~ ~

Fourth, I not sure how to explain that, Udon not so powerful in building large structures, it does not gives you feeling of real development environment. It feels morle like writing Windows commandline shell scripts, but visually. We working with concepts of "Objects", but we dont have fundamental concepts of object-oriented programming: encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism. You can not define own types, and even if it will be possible in future, it does not feels like it will be possible to extend types, use all power of polymorphism, which can be important for implementing complex game logics and mechanics. We can not even call Udon functional as it does not have "pure" functions! Yea, we have SubGraphs but we dont have contextual I/O for that. We need to set global instance variables and "call" subgraph using events (messages) which is really cringy. Can we get at least ok-implemented functions?

~ ~ ~

So my suggestions to improve:
- In Node Graphs: Make a lot of abstarctions and helper operations to make things actually simplier for newbies. May be "Udon commons library" or something.
- In Node Graphs: Make execution path for absolutely every node, so it's execution time and order will be explicit and obvious, even with even if you have to sacrifice convenience of "free nodes".
- In Node Graphs: Make easier read/write to local variables, for caching data in data flow to avoid unnecesary geters calls, also here:
- - Make nodes inputs/outputs not only flow lines and user-given statics, but also with inplace variable selector, so creators can read/write variables directly in node without creating tons of extra get/set nodes.
- In Node Graphs: Probably make nodes puzzle-like for execution path, so it's easier to control flow order. Or do something with flow control, to make it in way that gives less possibilities to do something wrong.
- If it's possible throw away ASM/VM and compile Udon nodes directly into CIL. Allow custom user-provided CIL asms. Validate CIL on both server and client for blacklisted/malicious operations using analysis tools. Setup kind of sandboxed environment using security API for creators scripts execution.
- If not, then make official and maintained way for compiling C#/CIL into Udon ASM, so community can write C# scripts without depending on 3rd tools. Improve Udon to be more close to CIL, with custom functions and types, with power of OOP concepts.
